opus-5.5.text:
I think my default advice is that most people should lean toward joining an existing organization, at least at first, and I'd want someone to have a pretty specific reason before they go the founder route.

Part of that is just that starting an organization is really hard, and it's hard in ways that don't have much to do with AI safety. You're suddenly spending a lot of your time on hiring, fundraising, management, operations, legal stuff, keeping people motivated. If what you're excited about is the actual research or the actual policy work, founding can pull you away from that for years. And early in your career you often don't yet have a good sense of what good work in the field looks like, what the bottlenecks really are, who the people are. You learn a lot of that by being inside an organization that's already doing the work.

There's also a question of whether the world actually needs another organization. Sometimes people want to start something because they have an idea that's maybe 20% different from what an existing group is doing, and I think in a lot of those cases the better move is to go to that group and push for the thing from the inside. Coordination costs in a small field are real, and every new org competes for the same limited pool of talent, funding, and attention.

That said, I don't want to be too discouraging, because some of the most important things that have happened have come from people starting new things. The cases where I'd be more enthusiastic look something like this: there's a clear gap that you can articulate, where you've actually checked and nobody is doing it, or the people who might do it have told you they won't. You have some reason to think you specifically are well positioned, maybe relevant experience, maybe a network, maybe a track record of getting things done. And ideally you've tested the idea in a cheap way first: a side project, a pilot, a small grant, something where you get real feedback before you commit to building an institution.

One framing I find useful is to ask: what's the smallest version of this I could try? A lot of good organizations started as one or two people doing a project, and they only became organizations once it was clear the work was valuable and needed more structure. That's often better than starting with the org chart and the fundraising pitch.

And I'd add, people are often bad at estimating their own fit for founding. It's worth getting honest feedback from people who've done it, and worth noticing whether the appeal is the work itself or more the idea of being a founder. Those can come apart.

So overall: join by default, learn a lot, keep an eye out for real gaps, and if you see one you're unusually suited to fill, test it small before going big.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, and my honest answer is that most people should probably default to joining an existing organisation, and the people who should start something new are mostly going to know who they are.

Let me unpack that a bit. The case for joining an existing org is that you learn a tremendous amount just by being around people who've already figured out a lot of the basic stuff. How do you run a team, how do you hire, how do you decide what's worth working on, how do you avoid the dozen failure modes that every new organisation hits. If you go in fresh and start your own thing, you're going to rediscover all of those lessons the hard way, and that's expensive. It's expensive in your time and it's expensive in the field's time, because resources get spent on an org that's basically reinventing things.

There's also a version of this where people overestimate how much the bottleneck is "there aren't enough organisations" versus "there aren't enough people who are really good at the thing." In AI safety specifically, I think the second one is much more the binding constraint. If you are great at technical alignment research, or great at policy analysis, or great at operations, there are existing places that would love to have you and where you could have a lot of impact on day one. The marginal value of a great person at a good org is really high.

That said, there are situations where starting something makes sense. One is when you've looked carefully and there's a genuine gap, something nobody is doing, and you've talked to the people who would plausibly do it and they've told you they're not going to. Another is when you have a specific idea or approach that existing orgs have considered and rejected, and you think they're wrong, and you've actually stress-tested that belief rather than just being annoyed that they didn't adopt your thing. And the third is more of a personality fit thing. Some people are just much more productive when they own the whole picture and set the agenda, and they're miserable and underperform inside somebody else's structure. If that's you, you should take it seriously, but I'd want you to be pretty confident, because a lot of people think that's them and it isn't.

The thing I'd really push on is: if you're thinking about starting something, spend some time inside a relevant organisation first, even if it's a year or two. Not because you need permission, but because you'll have a much better sense of what the actual problems are, you'll have relationships with people who can help you, and you'll be able to tell the difference between a gap that exists because nobody's noticed it and a gap that exists because it's a bad idea. Those look identical from the outside and they look very different from the inside.

And I'd add one more thing, which is that "starting an org" is sometimes a solution looking for a problem. People get attached to the idea of founding something because it's high status or feels ambitious. But the goal is to reduce the risks from AI, and the question should always be what's the highest-impact thing you can do toward that, and sometimes the answer is start something, and more often the answer is go be excellent at a thing that already exists and needs you.

astra-6.text:
I would start with the question of what you want to get done, rather than whether you want to start an organisation. Is there some particular work that you think is really important and isn’t happening? And why isn’t it happening? Is it because nobody has tried it, because it’s hard to fund, or because people who have looked into it think it won’t work? Those lead to pretty different decisions.

If you’re relatively new to the field, I think joining an existing organisation is often a very good default. You get to learn from people, understand what the actual bottlenecks are, and develop your own judgment without simultaneously having to hire people, raise money, and run an institution. Those are substantial demands on your time.

But I wouldn’t turn that into a rule that you should never start something. If you have a concrete idea, a reason to think you can execute it, and it doesn’t fit well within an existing organisation, that can be a very good reason to start one. Ideally, you can test the core idea on a small scale first. Can you produce something useful? Can you find collaborators? Can you get thoughtful people to engage with it?

So the thing I’d look for is a strong case for the work and for why it needs a new organisation. The fact that AI safety is important is a reason to contribute; it doesn’t, by itself, tell you which organisational structure will let you contribute most.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d generally encourage people to start by looking for an existing organisation where they can do useful work and learn a lot. Starting an organisation adds a whole set of jobs — recruiting, fundraising, management — that can take you away from the problem you actually wanted to work on. And if you’re new to the field, it can be hard to tell which gaps are real and which ones look like gaps because you don’t yet understand what other people are doing.

But I wouldn’t make that a blanket rule. The key question is: what do you want to do, and why does it need a new organisation? If you have a specific approach, you’ve talked to people who might support or challenge it, and there really isn’t a good home for it, that can be a strong reason to start something.

I’d also try to make the decision less binary. You can test a research project, work with a small team, or find an organisation willing to host you before building a whole institution. That gives you a chance to learn whether the idea is promising and whether you actually enjoy the work of making it happen.
